A: Human kidney core biopsy H&E from the reported child; the caption and in-text identify Echinococcus multilocularis-type laminated membrane, cystic structures, calcific/necrotic debris, dense fibrosis and effaced renal parenchyma, supporting alveolar echinococcosis despite the absence of liver involvement. B: Lower-right inset from the same kidney core biopsy; the captioned thin laminar membrane measured on trichrome stain is a specific histologic feature of alveolar echinococcosis in this patient. C: Upper-left insert shows a captioned scolex from the kidney core-biopsy block; a scolex is parasite-specific evidence supporting alveolar echinococcosis, although this feature is not present in the allowed findings vocabulary.

panels.figure_caption: Kidney core biopsy of a child with disseminated Echinococcus multilocularis infection without liver involvement, Canada, 2018. Shown are folded laminated membrane (short black arrows) encircling variable-sized cystic structures (black circles) containing calcified and necrotic debris and dense periparasitic fibrosis (long black arrows), in a background of chronic inflammation and fibrosis. No residual normal kidney parenchyma was seen (hematoxylin and eosin stain, original magnification × 40). Inset at lower right shows laminar membrane, 18–19.4 μm in thickness in a background of fibrosis (Masson trichrome, original magnification ×40). Insert at upper left shows scolex attached to the paraffin edge of the block (original magnification ×40).

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (a, b). a: Human liver biopsy histology (HE) from a patient with confirmed alveolar echinococcosis (positive E. multilocularis serology, article title and caption explicitly state alveolar echinococcosis). The image shows the characteristic multiloculated cyst with a germinal/laminated layer indicated by red arrows, and surrounding granulomatous demarcated necrosis as described in the text. Classic textbook histopathology of the disease. b: Human liver biopsy histology (PAS stain) from the same patient with confirmed alveolar echinococcosis. The PAS stain demonstrates the PAS-positive laminated cuticular/germinal membranes characteristic of Echinococcus multilocularis infection, with red arrows indicating the membranes. Disease attribution is explicit in the caption and supported by positive serology in the text.

Therefore, a liver biopsy was performed, showing granulomatous demarcated necrosis zones and evidence of amorphous cuticular membranes with periodic acid-Schiff (PAS)-positivity compatible with Echinococcus spp. infestation (Figure 2). Malignancy could be excluded. The serology testing for Echinococcus multilocularis was positive (Table 1).
